From the St. James's Chronicle , March. 14. li is slated in a loiter from Calcutta of the 20th of January, written for the chance of reaching Bombay in time for the steamer, that the expedition preparing for China would consist of tiie following troops. From Bengal her Majesty's 21st and 26th regiments. with two regiments of native infantry. From Madras one of the þÿQueen s, and four of Native Infantry, with a regiment of Artillery and one of Engineers. From Ceylon one þÿQueen r s egiment. The whole were to be commanded by General Arbuthnot from Ceylon, and Generals Oglander and Walker to command divisions. Shipping to the extent of 4000 tons had been already taken up at Calcutta. Salt provisions were likely to be required to a considerable extent in China þÿ Times.

Bombay, Jan. 31 The most important feature in the intelligence bv the present mail is the immediate adoption, on the part of the government of India, of hostile measures against China, consequent upon instructions to that efftet from her þÿMajesty government s to Lord Auckland, received by the London November mail. The precise nature of the instructions lias not transpired, but it is generally believed that he has received peremptory orders to adopt extreme measures þÿ in other words, to declare war þÿ against Chiua. The Bengal government have issued tenders for 14,000 tons of shipping, and it is said that a considerable force þÿ according to some seven regiments, others say a more formidable armament þÿ is about to be dispatched from Calcutta and Madras immediately, to be cooperated with by a naval force of one 80 and two 74-gun ships, with an accompaniment of six frigates and smaller craft, partly to be supplied from the squadron on the India station. with a reinforcement from England. It is also rumoured, with what degree of probability 1 have not yet been able to learn, that Lord Auckland will forthwith proceed as Ambassador Plenipotentiary to China. With regard to the exact details of the expedition there is vet some uncertainty, but of the expedition itself none. The intelligence from China which reached to the 15th of December, continues to be of great interest. Jt appears that, in obedience to an express order ot the Emperor, the British trade with China, direct and indirect,

is to he stopped þÿ for þÿever None of the British shipping (with one solitary exception, the Thomas Coutts) had proceeded inside the Bogue, or would submit to sign the obnoxious bond. The vessels accordingly remained outside, and their cargoes were transhipped in American vessels to Whampoa, for which an enormous freight was charged, lately as much as eight dollars per bale for cotton Several British vessels were also solii to the Americans, and are now under the flag of that nation. The imperial Commissioner Lin, however, issued an edict peremptorily putting a stop to the purchase of vessels from the English by the Americans or others, and also all transhipment of Br itish property into American or any other vessels ; and further, that if the British shipping outside did not go up to Whampoa belore the 6th of December, and conform to the rules laid down, the trade with the English nation

wm mm should terminate for ever Raw cotton in bales, and a variety of Indian and British staple ai tides, are now as illegal to import as opium. The licensed passage-boats are also entirely interdicted from entering Can ton river. The prohibition of imports extends to Macao, and three mandarins of rank were on their way to enforce it. A coadjutor to Liu (a Tartar) was expected to arrive And the remaining þÿJ arsees,Moormen, and other natives of India, being British subjects, were to have been expelled from Canton on the 6th.

Bombay, Jan 31. The East Indies are now at peace, for the designing schemes of Russia have been fully defeated by the activity and energy of the Indian government. The newly-conquered districts, which are larger than France and Belgium together, are tranquil. Lord Keane, who went on a visit to the Court of Lahore, is now on his return, covered with glory, by the Indus river, to Bombay. The Bengal army is going back to that Presidency, and those regiments of the Bombay army which can be spared from the newly acquired provinces on the Indus are also on their return to this eitv The Governor General of India (Lord Auckland), who had intended to fix his residence this year in the centre of India, having received instructions from London, suddenly set out for Calcutta, where orders have been issued to make ready an expedition against China. By a most fortunate coincidence Sir J. J. Bremer Gordon, who by the death oi Admiral Maitland became the senior otiioer of the Indian squadron, appeared on the 17th off Madras, having, in compliance with orders issued by the late admiral, come from Syd uey. This gallant officer, who will act in conformity with Lord Auckland, has taken the command of the squadron, which consists of the Volage 28. and the Hyacinth 18, now in the Chinese seas; oftheCiuiscr 18, now in the Straits; of the Weilesley 71, the C.m way 28, the Alligator 26, the Childers 18, the Larne 18, and the Algerine 10, at various stations on the coast of India. The Druid 44, is expected also from Ae» Zealand þÿ

Coals are to be sent to an island near China Sapata is mentioned as the station, but as being a barren rock, great doubt is entertained of its being selected. In the beginning of November, when 30 war junks attempted to aitaek the Biinslt þÿnv. n ot war at Chuenpee, which were spee dilv dispersed, five or six were sunk, -anti t he Chinese admiral so desperately wounded that he has since died. Lin sent off a the express to Pekin for further instructions. Another commissioner has since come to his aid, arid there is, it is said, a disposition to treat, notwithstanding the stoppage of the trade for ever. Tin Chinese government is by this time informed of the results of the late campaigns in India.

Proclamation from flie Commissioner ami tlie þÿGovernor stopping for ever l lie Knglisli Trade. þÿ Lin, High Imperial Commissioner, and Tang, Governor of the þÿ7 aon wang, issue these for the purpose of giving plain information. þÿ It appears on record than we the Commissioner and the Governor, upon the 15th of November, respectively received the following imperial commands þÿ -

mmmm OT5ST®! þÿ The execution bv the foreign ships of the duly prepared earnest bond, if, indeed, it can be depended on, will naturally bring about a gradual and entire cleansing away of the opium. But if any further change fulness be shown by those foreign vessels, it will be requisite that the martial terrors be displayed to them ; that they be for ever disallowed intercourse of trade, to the end that the blind perverse tribe may konw when to take warning and to be afraid. But ships of all other foreign nations that subscribe ihe pro. scribed form ol bond they are allowed to hold commerce with Thus we would admonish and punish, and so separate the good from the evil. They are not allowed to suffer the English clandestinely to combine with them, nor are they to convey the English vessels, or their cargoes, either under the guise of changed names or as their carriers, to he disposed of for them. By so doing they will when they shall be discovered, involve a like cutting off of their own trade. This is in obedience to the imperial pleasure, wiih t ho object of for ever cutting off the import of opium, and of warning and cautioning the changeful temper of the foreigners. From the New Yurk Albion. April 4, 1840. We have copied to-dav the latest correspondence between Mr. Fox the British minister at Washington and the Government of the United States, a perusal of which will apprize the reader of t fie posture of affairs in relation to the Northeastern Boundary at the present moment. The merits of this question we have discussed so often, that it is scarcely necessary to revert to that branch of the subject again ; let us rather devote ourselves to the inculcations of peace and concord. We have always said that this question was too insignificant to disturb the peaceful relations of the two countries, and we again say that no adequate cause even now exists for aught that can place them in danger. The portion of the disputed territory really in contention is of small value, for England has already offered to concede half, which hail contains all the best of the timber, and the most valuable part of the territory in other respects. The land north of the River St John is essential to Great Britain in order to keep up her communication with Canada, hut to the United States it is not worth perhaps a quarter of a dollar per acre. To England it is of political, but to the United States of only commercial value. The latter could sustain no loss of national honour bv relin mishing a portion of the claim in this quarter if done by fair and honorable diplomatic negotiation. The correspondence intimates the desire still felt by Mr. Van Buren to submit the question once more to the arbitrament of a

third power. To such a course few can have any objection, provided the State of Maine will, on this occasion, abide by the decision. The treaty of Ghent provides for this mode of adjustment should other means fail, and it is expedient, and always more satisfactory, in such cases, to follow the injunctions of such instruments. Let us then resubmit the question good faith, in and in the spit it of justice let each party abide the result. But it is assumed bv some of our contemporaries, that England unwilling again is " to stand the hazard ol the die." This is excusable, for having abided by it once and the opposite patty refusing its assent because the decision was not congenial to its own views þÿ Arms and þÿMunitions it perhaps is not fair to ask ths first party again to yield itself up to the uncertainty of a new
haws at r»OTrw»!r?sat wiiiii ii ! iiimiiiiwiiiiw iii mi ii iiiiiiiiiiiiiiii lain mi ii i ii iimw n m mrinrnninrnTrfi

trial But the reluctance might be overcome if the following condition were appended þÿ namely, that should the verdict lie adverse to Great Britain þÿ she should have the option o .! purchasing such portion of the territory north of the St John, at a given price, as would secure her a communication with the upper provinces. By this plan the United States would sustain no disadvantage, for on that side of the river their jurisdiction has never extended. The Americans have no fortifications there, nor is there a single American settler to be found in the whole region We can see no possible objection to such a basis of the settlement, and sincerely hope that it, or one somewhat resembling it, may be adopted. At all events we trust that nothing will be done bv the state or people of Maine to widen the breath, and that ajust deference will be paid to the authority of the Government of the United States, which alone lias the constitutional power to declare war or to make peace. If Governor Fairfield will not retire from his position and the block houses he has erected at the mouth of Fish river, may not it be equitable call to for the removal of the 175 British tt oops on Temisquata Lake. The latter are not within one hundred miles of any American settlement, and 175 red coats 100 hundred miles off, ought not to cause alarm to the Sovereign State of Maine Let it be understood that neither party shall advance further, or assume any new or hostile altitude, and all will be well. We never saw a case in which

there was less real cause of discoid. The tenor of Mr. Forsyth's last letter is moderate, and, with the well known pacific intentions of the President, and the unwillingness that exists on the other side to plunge into war, lead us fervently to hope that the dark hour will speedily pass away, and be succeeded by the sun shine of peace, happiness, and prosperity of both nations. It is a great error to suppose that the government and people of England are anxious for war. All the great interests of the country are deepiy pledged to maintain peace. þÿ Let us see who, in Great Britain would abjure hostilities at this moment with this country. 1. The Tory journals, however, are earefui not to let slip the opportunity which the actual posture of affairs seems to alfird them of venting their base and factious malignity against our rulers, not because thev are about to engage the country in hostilites with a distant enemv, but because they profess Liberal principles, and, while they defend the interest and honour of the nation abroad, are anxious to promote its freedom and prosperity at home. It has long been objected to the instruments of this unpatriotic faction, that by their perverse and wicked misrepresentations, by exaggerating our domestic difficulties, by depreciating our naval strength þÿ in short, bv describing the empire as ready to fall to pieces from the operation of internal decay, they actively encourage and incite foreign powers to attack us. in the persuasion that if our condition be such as is depicted by these traitors, we must easily become their prev Thus, on Friday last, whilst giving publicity to the faets which justify, nav, imperatively call for, the war witii China, the Times, delightedly and laboriously enumerated the various sources of

perplexity an I danger which at present encompass the empire, chuckling with pleasure as it set down each of them, and rejoicing at the fancied prospect of national humiliations and disasters. liut let it he that we are threatened with war in North America; admit that France will seize eagerlv upon the opportunity of pushing its conquests in Northern Africa ; grant that Russia will establish herself in Khiva; what then? þÿ would any one of these events he warded off, or even delayed, by our tamely submitting to insults front the Chinese, and not using o the most favourable occasion that may ever perhaps occur of subduing and taking possession of that empire þÿ for, to this in all probability the present movement will lead ? On the contrary, we can assure the factious and un- English journalist, that nothing that could possibly happen would inflict upon our enemies a pain so deep and lasting as the beholding ns in possession of the Chinese empire. While the United States may be exposing itself to los« and defeat in search of a few marshy acres on the Maine frontier þÿ while France is entailing on itself endless and useless expense, in its abortive attempt at introducing cufi's <jj- viudivil/es into Northern Africa, whilst Russia is burying its bravest soldiers in the sands of the Barsak Steppe

and the pestilential marshes of t he Oxuv, (Leal Brit ain is opening up to itself a way to the possession of one of the largest and finest countries on the hani'ahle globe ; and that, if we undertake the enterprise we shall, with tne assistance ol Divine Providence, bring it to a successful close I here can bo no doubt. For, although it may be true, as Captain Elliot in his communication to government insists, that the military character of the Chinese and the military resources of their country, are not so contemptible as certain travellers have representee them, still the facj is indisputable that they are inferior as soldiers 10 the Affghangs, to the Pattans. to the Kohillus, to the Rajpoots, to the Alahrattasi to the Burmese, over each and all of whom we have successively triumphed ; and their empire, whatever persons ignorant of geography may pretend, is less populous, less powerful, less capable of defence than that Indian empire which is already to all intents and purposes our own, from the Hindoo lvoosh to Cape Coniorin. And vet observe the tone of simplicity in which the leading Tory journal speaks of the circumstances of the approaching war. " The conveyance, the subsistence, the wants, the reinforcement ol a corps of 1(5,000 men in such a climate carrying on an unknown description of warfare at from 1,500 miles distant from its embaroation, and against a population of perhaps 200,0il0,000, whose belligerent qualities, as Captain Elliot declares to Lord Palmer-

ston, have been extremely underrated, are considerations of no trivial kind" From this it is as clear as day that the Times misunderstands the state of the case altogether. In the first place there can be no doubt that by making use of the phrase "such a climate," the limes would insinuate that China is an unhealthy country, while the fact is that the climate is mild and salubrious, far more so then the places from which the troops are to lie transported thither. Secondly, with respect to population, it was satisfactorily shown before I'arliament in 1830, that the Chinese empire is less populous than Hindustan the greatest possible amount of its population being about one hundred and thirty millions ; and if the nature of the country and the government be taken into consideration, it will be admitted that even this is a tolerably high number. For, as they who have diligently examined the travels of the Jesuits well know, there exist vast sandy deserts, not only on the frontiers of Thibet and Mongolia, but here and there in the very heart of the empire, and that every where, at a little distance from the rivers and great canals, there are large tracts of uncultivated lands, rendered uninhabited by the tyranny of the government. Even were it quite otherwise, however, and if the population amount, according to the fancy of the old geographers, to three hundred and thirtythree millions, neither more nor less, still this circumstances would oppose no difficulties whatever in the way of our conquest, for

were the world itself peopled with Chinese, it would be an easy matter for Great Britain to erect a universal empire. But before conjuring up before its imagination all the ditliculties, the existence of which is implied in the above paragraph, the Tory journalist should have inquired a little into the actual slate ol China. He would then probably have found that nut ol the two hundred mil-

lions of people which he s ' berally appro priates to the Chinese monarchy, at leas! one hundred and seventy millions ate !>y birth and feeling inimical to the government, i or the emperor being a foreigner, h s troops being foreign, and the spirit of h:s r e altogether un-Clnnese, while numerous scions o! the old royal family are still scattered over 'ne country, living in danger and obscurity, hut > i cherishing their pretensions to the crone we need only set up one of these princ-s a a rival to the reigning emperor, a Mantchoo Tartar, to kindle a civil war from Canton to the Great Wall. From the þÿ St. James's Chronicle' Way 19. Malta papers, the Medilerranet, the Portafoglio, and the Times , to the 7th iust , along with a letter from our private correspondent of that þÿday s date, have reached us this morning, and bring news of some interest from Naples. The King of the Two Sicilies, having admitted the principle upon which the demands of the British government are founded, has ollered to submit the question of the amount of compensation to be paid to England to the French government; which offer has been accepted by the British minister, on the express condition that the matter be definitively settled in three weeks. The embargoes on both sides have been withdrawn

Sir Robert Stopford has directed the release all the Neapolitan vessels which have been sent into Malta, four in number, one with a neutral freight. Admiral Lalendo and the French squadron were at Smyrna on the 30th. Admiral Kosamel was expected there daily, to take the chief command of the French fleet, which would then consist of 13 ships of the line, two corvettes, five brigs, and two steamers.

The Monileur of Friday contains a telegraphic dispatch from Toulon, dated May 13, conveying advices from Cherchell to May the 9th, from which it appears that whilst the French army in Africa, under Marshal Valle, had gained no advantage of the slightest importance, the Arabs had exhibited a degree of energy and activity w hich lot bids the expectation that they will be easily subdued. That the result will finally be in favour of the French, however, appears to be tiie universal impression in Farts; but that the triumph will cost incomparably more than it is worth, does not seem to be questioned. In the Chamber of Deputies on Friday, the declaration of M. Thiers, that France was resolved, cou/e qui coute, to maintain her conquests in Africa, but neither to consolidate nor extend them, appears to have overborne all opposition, aud to have secured the success of the project of law tor extraordinary credits for that service for 1839, by a majority of 261 to 68. In the Chamber of Deputies on Saturday M. Thiers, who seems to regard the improvement in our mode of communication with America with no little jealousy, brought in a bill to carry out a project of transatlantic steam navigation, from Havre, Bordeaux, and Marseilles. The Havre packets will, it is proposed, communicate with New York, and will be the only series which will be left in the hands of private speculators. The company is, however, to be assisted by an annual allowance of 12.000.000 francs from the government. The Bourdeaux and Mar-

seilles lines are to be undertaken at the expense of the stale. Sixteen steamers, of from 220 to 450 horse power, are to be constructed at the public expense ; for which purpose a vote of 25 millions of francs is proposed, payable in the next three years. What will Lord Minto and his parasytes say to this large addition to the war steamers of France, so constructed as to admit of their receiving the formidable þÿPaixhans gun, and other descriptions of armament, as occasion may arise.

Rosas has been re-elected for five years. PARIS, May 24. We find in the Commerce a letter, dated Naples, the 11th iust., stating that the King, alarmed at the unfavoiable accounts which daily reached him Irom Sicily, embarked with the Queen for that island, during the night of the 10th, in the Ferdtuando Frimo steamer. The mystery attending the departure ol their Majesties had given use to many conjectures, aud it was thought that a plan for a general insurrection had been discovered, aud that the ministry had deemed the presence of the King necessary to prevent an explosion. The discontent, it appears, was not confined to the people. The nobility were beginning to murmur, and to claim the privileges guaranteed to Sicily by the treaty of Vienna, which were abolished by King Ferdinand l. Their Majesties were to return to Naples in the course of a fortnight. The Alexandria correspondent of the Augsburg Gazette writes, under date of the 26th ult,, that Lord Keane had been treated with the greatest distinction by Mehemet Ali on his passage through that city. Nothing new had reached ft om Sv ria. Jin a him i aeha had transferred this head quarters to Aleppo, and Soliman Facha remained at St. Jean þÿd Acre. Levies of recruits still continued, and the preparations ol defence were carried on with unabated activity The officers of
the Alexandria National Guard were presented to the Viceroy on the 24th, by their General, Said el Garbi.

Le Commerce contains a long article on the affairs of La Flata, in which Admiral Dupotet is strongly reprimanded for accepting the mediation of Mr. Manderville, the British Consul in Buenos Ayres. According to that journal, the following are the preliminaries agreed to between the French Admiral and Don Felipe Arana, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Rosas : þÿ þÿ 1. The Argentine confederation shall send a Plenipotentiary Minister to his Majesty the King of the French, to settle the differences which have arisen, between the two countries. þÿ 2. The blockade shall be immediately raised, and the island of Martin oarcia restored, together with all its warlike materials, artillery, &c. þÿ 3. In the meanwhile, the French shall be treated in Buenos Ayres on the same footing as foreigners are in France. þÿ 4. The indemnities claimed by .French citizens shall be regulated in France by the Argentine envoy. þÿ 5. The arms, warlike ammunition, &c., which the Admiral or French agents have furnished to the revolters, who disturb public peace and attack the lawful government of Rosas, shall be withdiawn within 40 þÿday3.

May 28. Accounts from China, which have been received via U. Stales state þÿ that the Portuguese at Macao have sent guns and men to aid the Chinese in defending the forts at the Bogue against the British ships; and the consequence will be, in all probability, a , bombardment of Macao by the English squad-

ron in addition to the for' at the Bojjue. The Chinese have thrown a strong raft, well secured by heavy chains, across the stream ; on this a large force of men armed are placed, and vessels are permitted to pass through an opening which is made for them bv letting one or more of the rails swing with the tide."

The French journals, both of Paris and the South of France, seem to take premature alarm at the state of affairs of Naples, representing the King as still recalcitrant, and England as still threatening. The Augsburg Gazette, on the contrary, represents the King of Naples as having abandoned the deference to the mediation of France, and couriers as having been sent to Paris with full statements, likely to bring in return a decision The King and Queen of Naples had gone to Sicily, where late events no doubt required his presence. Malta letters of the 16th, however, represent Admiral Stopford as having orders to sail to Naples with two ships of the line, a frigate and a steamer.

PARIS, May 25. In the Chamber of Deputies to day the bill voting sums for canals was carried by a majority of 211 against 103. The order of the day was the debate on the project of law for the removal of the remains ol Napoleon, which was opened by M. Glais Bizoin, who said that his vote would have been a silent one if the committee had simply demanded a grant, but as there seemed to be an intention of endeavouring to excite a Bonapartian mania, in favour certainly of a great captain and a great genious, he could only say he was of evil as well as of good. He had no w ish to attack the glory of the empire, for it was that ot France ; but something ought also to be said in favour of the attachment to a liberal and constitutional government The greatest blessing from Providence was, in Ins humble opinion, not only to France, but to Europe, the tall of the Imperial regime, and he would use all his influence to preserve his country from such a sy stem, and in this course he would have with him the majority of the nation. He rejected energetically this mode or fashion of crying up the empire, and he was decidedly opposed to the statue of Napoleon being removed from thp Vendome column to erect an cuquestrian one in some public place He thought that his homage was not justified, as it appertained solely to monarchs. M. Gaugain supported the project, but did not approve of the choice of the Invalides, as the Madeleine ought to have received the remains.

A few days ago all France was ringing with enthusiastic approbation of the glorious leon to the country which had been the Napo- project of transferring the remains of theatre of his genius In the Chamber of Deputies the proposition had been carried by acclamation. þÿ1 ranee appeared to be animated by but one feeling þÿ one voice on the subject. As for the journalists, they were in raptures. The tardy buf grateful homage about to be rendered to the memory ofNapoleon had somealmost of the sublime. No later than partake thing in it which appeared to them to Tuesday last, however, the Chamber of Deputies, economical even in its enthusiasm, reduced the sum recommended bv the committee for carrying out this universally popular suggestion from two millions of francs to one, thus depriving the affair of at least one-half of the eclat which would otherwise attach to it. After reducing the amount proposed by the committee from two millions to one, þÿthe article providing for the erection of an equestrian statue of Napoleon was rejected; and the ensemble ol the bill was voted by a majority ol 280 against 65, leaving' the measure in the position in which it was oitgiualiy introduced by the ministry.

LONDON, May 31. Appointment of married men in the Army, þÿ A .non j- tiie regulations of the War Department respecting the appointment in the army of persons from civil life, there is one stating that no candidate will be examined who is married. The Army and Navy Chronicle of the 23d instant publishes an extract from a Report made to t lie Secretary of War giving the reasons of this regulation. It is stated that the pay of a second lieutenant, about 78i) dollars a year, is not more than adequate to lus ovvii support in the dress and appearance which his profession requires; his transportation allowance of ten cents per mile will not do more than pay his individual travelling expenses; his quarters when in garrison are loo small lor the accommodation of a family ; and the duties of the younger oliicers require their presence almost continually with their companies in the field. þÿ These considerations it is thought are suffi. ciently strong to authorise the adoption ol the above named regulation.

The ship was abandoned about ten þÿo clock, the on Monday morning, at which time the fire was rapidly increasing, and the decks getting hotter every minute. When Captain Anthony left her with her passengers and crew, tfie wind was blowing almost a gale þÿ so hard, that the Clifton was compelled to be kept under double reefed topsails. The sea, too, was very rough. When the alarm was first given, the ship was hove to, to prevent a too rapid spread of the fire, and for the purpose of devoting more attention to quenching it. Attempts were made to descend to where it was burning, hut they proved unsuccessful, in consequence of the dense smoke and strong sulpharic smell. When the vessel was struck, she was in longitude 58, but was drifted and blown to Ion. 56, where she was fallen in with. The ladies behaved nobly, and Captain Anthony states, that they were willing to do any thing, to be placed any where & uttered not a word of fear, but were an example to all the rest. þÿ Whilst they were in the boat, he would occasionally send them hot coffee, roast chickens, and such like things. Wiih one or two exceptions, there was nothing saved except what the passengers and crew had on their backs. One of the ladies saved two dresses in a carpet bag, but all were intent in stowing provisions in the boats. The steward, however, saved the þÿcaptain t s runk, and one box of specie, containing six hundred dollars. The ladies had on thick comfortable dresses at the time of the accident, and also cloaks. The other passengers were also dressed warmly, but they were completely drenched with water. a>AiT3:g. From Btlft Weekly ilestenger, June 13. ATROCIOUS ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE THE QUEEN and PRINCE ALBERT.

About six o'clock on Wednesday evening the Queen and Prince Albert left Buckingham Palace bv the garden gate opening upon Constitution hill Her Majesty and the Prince were seated in a very low German drotschky, followed bv the Equerries in Watting, Colonel Buckley and Sir Edward Bowater, and the usual attendants on horseback. A number of respectable people had assembled outside the gate to witness their departure, and were ranged in two lines to admit of the carriages passing through. After the carriage had issued from the gate, and had proceeded some short distance up Constitution-hill, so as to be quite clear of the crowd, a young man, who it is said had come from the Green Park, and was standing with his back to the railings, presented pistol and fired it directly, either a at her Majesty or Prince Albert, there being no person between him and the carriage. þÿ The Prince, who, it would seem, had heard the whistling of the ball, turned his head in the direction from which the report came, and her Majesty at the same instant rose up in the carriage, but Prince Albert as suddenly pulled her down by his side. The man then drew from behind his back a second pistol, which he discharged after the carriage, which proceeding at the ordinary pace, had by that time passed him a little. The reports of both pistols were very loud, and at the discharge of the second some of the female spectators screamed loudly. Several persons rushed towards the perpretator of this gross outrage,

and he was immediately seized, first by a person having the appearance of a labouring man, and then bv Mr. Beckham, one of the Queen's pages, and another bystander, by whom he was handed over to two of the metropolitan police, who conveyed him to the Queensquare Police Court. By some it is alleged that the miscreant stood with his arms folded, apparently waiting for the arrival of the carriage ; others state, that he was seen croaching down, as if endeavouring to escape observation ; and that, after firing the first shot, he changed the second pistol into his right hand in order to fire it. The discharge of the pistols and the seizure of the offender scarcely occupied a minute. Her Majestv's carriage sustained no delay, and moved on up Constitution hill at the usual pace, and by half- past six had arrived at the Uuchess of Kents, Ingestrie House, Belgrave square, where her Majesty stopped for a short time, but neither her appearance nor that ol Prince Albert evinced any indication of alarm or excitement at the deadly attack from which they had so providentially escaped. I he name of the ruffian who has been guilty of this atrocious attack is Edward Oxford. His appearance is that of a mechanic, Irom 18 to 20 years of age, and rather below the middle height. We have been informed that on searching him a list of the names of 26 individuals was found, which he admitted that he intended to have burnt or destroyed, and some circumstance has transpired which leads to a belief that the persons whose names
are contained in the list above-mentioned are 1

raasiimasma ATI3 in some way connected with the prisoner for some sinister purpose. On searching his lodgings a sword was also found, and some crape arranged for the purpose of being worn on a hat or a cap in such a way as to conceal the face of the wearer, and the crape is also stated to be folded in a peculiar manner, so that the crape which was intended for the prisoner would distinguish him from the rest of the gang with which it is said he is connected , and who were to be similarly disguised. VV e have also heard that on being taken to the police-station the following conversation took place : þÿ " What are you ? þÿ 1 have been brought up to the bar. " Do you mean to say as a lawyer ? þÿ No ; to the bar, to draw porter. " Are you a potboy ? þÿ No, I'm above that. as " Are you publican ? þÿ that " No, I'm not so high We cannot vouch for the authenticity of this conversation, but merely give it as it reached us. The conduct of the prisoner throughout his examination mandested great self-possession. The pistols are described as small pistols of Birmingham manufacture, rather well fin ished. They were loaded with balls, one of which struck the wall opposite to where the prisoner stood, and the other ball is said to have lodged one of the trees. in

RE APPEARANCE IN PUBLIC OF HER MAJESTV AMI PRINCE At. BERT. It being understood that her Majesty and Prince Albert would take their accustomed drive this evening in the Parks, notwithstanding the occurrence of yesterday, a large assemblage of persons took place in the vicinity of Buckingham Palace. At a few minuies after six the garden gates were opened, and the outriders appeared. þÿ This was the signal for a general rush to this point, and the instant her Majesty's carriage was seen the cheering became tremendous, and her Majesty and the piince were completely surrounded by her Majesty's loyal and loving subjects, who greeted them both in the most enthusiastic manner. The Queen looked remarkably well, and acknowledged the congratulations of her people by icpeatedly bowing, while Prince Albert continued to taise his hat as he passed through the throng, which, on horse and foot, all but impeded the progress of the royal party. About half an hour before the appearance of her Majesty, one of the pistol balls was found by two boys, who were looking at the marks in the wall. The ball was of large size, and completely flattened, on one side bearing marks resembling the impression of the bricks. The lads were about to walk off' with the ball as a curiosity, when Mr. Manning, of 13, Great Portland-street, Cavendish square, an officer in her Majesty's service, who was passing at the time, and heard of the discovery, took both the boys and the ball to the palace, when the ball was given

into the custody of the inspector on duty, and the lads were by him shortly afterwards taken to the police-station in Gardener's lane, in order that their evidence of the discovery of the ball might be communicated in the proper quarter. The reception which her Majesty received on her arrival in Hyde-Park exceeds all that wc have ever witnessed in the way of enthu-

siastic display of feeling ; and the number which thronged the drive in the park have perhaps never been equalled. The re appearance of her Majesty and the Prince had highly gratified the public, who longed for an opportunity of displaying their sympathy with her Majesty under the painfully exciting circumstances ol the murderous attempt upon her life. The palace gates from twelve o'clock at noon until nine in the evening were completely besieged by the carriages of the nobility who entered the lodge and wrote their names in the book. It were useless to particularise names, for " all" were there. From the coolness exhibited by the prisoner when apprehended, and his apparent indifference as to the result of the serious charge upon which he was taken into custody, it wag thought that his mind was not at all disturbed by the perilous situation in which he had placed himself by the dreadful act he had attempted to commit; but those who have had an opportunity of conversing with him, and observing him closely, say that at times he evinced considerably anxiety about the matter, and could not well conceal his agitationlie spoke freely about what he had done, and answered any questions put to him in the most careless manner; but when the conversation dropped he appeared disturbed, and that his agitation might not he noticed he frequently commenced to whistle, and it was evidently difficult for him to assume that carelessness which has been rcmaiked in his be-

haviour. In speaking to one of the officers about the riots at Birmingham, he observed that the chartists had been taken by surprise, hut he never said a word to lead to the belief that he had ever any connection with them þÿ He stated, however, that he considered the Queen unfit to reign over the English people, but he gave no reason for thinking so, nor did he at all allude to politics in his conversations. On learning that the officer bad accompanied the carriage on its return to the palace, he inquired how her Majesty and Prince Albert looked, and the officer told him that he ohsered nothing particular in their appearance. " Did they not appear alarmed ?" he inquired. " No, not in the least alarmed," was the answer. " Had you seen Prince Albert I" he then said, « I could see he was alarmed When I fired the first shot he looked towards me, and put out his foot, as if he intended to seize me, but when I drew out the second pistol and presented it, he was afraid, and did not attempt to do anything farther." At another lime he spoke of the manner in which he was apprehended, and endeavoured to appear amused at the anxiety exhibited by every one to take into custody the individual who fired the shots. Edward Oxford is the son of a jeweller. His father has been dead about eight years, and bis mother subsequently kept a coffe shop in the Waterloo-road, opposite the York, hotel, which she left about three years since. Oxford is a native of Birmingham, which he left about three years since, and went to

reside with Ins aunt, Mrs. Powell, who then kept the King's Head at Hounslow. There he was considered a very forward boy. From Hounslow he came to London, and entered the service of Mr. Minton, licensed victualler, and then proprietor of the Shepherd and Flock, High-street, nearly facing the Police-court, Marylcbane, in which houe

he remained, with some intermission, about a year ami a half. His situation was that of barman; a young man named William H izelwood was also there in the same capacity, but they could not agree, and the quarrels which frequently took plane between them assumed a serious character. Hazelwood states, that on more than one occasion Oxford (the intendi d regicide) thieatened to stab him, and was once about to put his threat into execution ; they were both in the kitchen when some words arose between thein, and in the heat of passion Oxford ran towards him with a knife. Hazelwood in a very resolute manner, seized hold of the arm of his assailant, when he succeeded in wresting the weapon from him, and knocked him down. Much ill will existed between them, and eventually Mr Minton, who, however, is stated to have been partial to Oxford, discharged him. Subsequently he was in great distress, and was occasionally employed by Mr. Minton; and Hazelwood leaving Mr. Mutton's service, Oxford was reinstated in his former situation, and continued therein many months, to the entire satisfaction of the landlord. Many persons who were in the frequent habit of being served by him have described him to be of a sullen temper, and very reserved in his actions.

The battered bullet which was found by the two boys, and which is now in the possession of Inspector Partridge, of the A division, is a much larger one than could have been fired out of the pistols taken from the prisoner. It must have been dropped near the broken wall by design or accident, as the police removed a number of wheelbarrows full of loose gravel or drift to the palace, where it was carefully sifted, and afterwards made a minute examination of the adjoining ground. Besides, it is the prevailing opinion of both military and civil officers who have inspected the wall, that the indentation was not made with a pistol-ball.

The prisoner, Oxford, it appears, was in the habit of frequenting Mr Green's shootinggallery in Leicester-square ; but it is not true that the gentlemen who go there mixed in company with him. On the contrary, they avoided him in consequence of his youth and plebian appearance. His custom was to spend Is. at the gallery upon each visit, and he generally divided that sum in the practice ol pistol and rifle shooting. In the use of the latter, it is stated, he was much more expert than in the former, it was also ascertained for certainty, that, upon the occasion of his last visit, he purchased of Mr. Green a dozen pistol bullets, and the officers now have a ball of a corresponding size in their possession. The letters and treasonable papers found at the same place bear no post mark, and notwiihsiaiiding the most minute and searching investigation 011 the part ol the officers, they had not been able to find out at a late hour last night where the unlawful society of " Young England" held their meetings.

The rules of the society(12 in number) are of a most treasonable character, and are not printed, but writleu on two sheets of foolscap, bearing a similar water-mark to the government paper. It would seem that the prisoner held an important sintioa in this wretched society not only from iiis erape cap which was touud being decorated with ribbons, but also from his slvimg iunisdl " Young England."

From Ball's Weekly Messenger, June 13. We have to state the arrival of two extraordinary expresses from India, bringing journals and dispatches from Bombay down to the 30th of April, and intelligence from China up to the 13th of March, that is, within three months of the present time. The substance of these accounts is, summarily, that the British expedition from India to China had embarked at Madras on the Itith of April, and that the ships and troops were on their voyage, in the first instance, for the Canton river. On their side the Chinese displayed fierce activity and a stubborn malignant determination. The accounts from China brought Vv these papers and correspondence come down to the 13th of March. They state that an order of the Emperor for suspending trade with all foreign nations, without exception, reached Canton on the 12th of February. The Emperor, moreover, ordered Commissioner Ein to give effect to that interdict, without referring to the government at Pekin. The accounts then proceed to state that the utmost alarm prevailed at Macao, which had been greatly increased bv two or more successive attempts of the Chinese viceroy to burn the British fleet in Tongkoo Bay. The first of tiiese attempis appears to have been made on the 9th of February, and is very pictuiesquely described in one of the dispatches It appears that about half-past one o'clock on Saturday morning, some Chinese fire-ships were observed coming down from the end of the bay in flames, but tiie wind having shifted against them, they drifted in-

shore ot the shipping through the mass of Sinai! Chinese boats arid foreign schooners ; one touched the Devil schoouer, and set fiie to her tor ward, but the crew succeeded in extinguishing the fire with the loss of the jib and damage to the bowsprit. These junks, or ratts, were filled with all kind of combustibles, cotton, oil, bamboo guns, or rather tubes, thickly mounted in several tiers, which threw out fire balls as the fire reached them. Some of the ships slipped their cables, and one of them was aground for a few hours, but without receiving any damage. It was the opinion of an experienced eye-witness that had there been 20 such junks chained together, the shipping would have been greatly injured. This abortive attempt, however, had the good effect of awakening the captains and officers of the ships to the danger to which they arc exposed, and they are therefore more on the alert ; several having bent sails, shifted their berths, and got springs on their cables. It is added in a later statement that the boats of her Majesty's ship Volage were employed in towing these fire ships out of the line of danger. They burnt out, after having drifted on shore without explosion, though, it is said, they were filled with bamboos stuffed with gunpowder, broken glass, small stones, <fcc. On the following O nb'ht O another attempt at firing the fleet was made, but without success The tide was very low, and the weather fine, two circumstances much in favour of the fleet, which might have suf-

fered considerably had the attempt of the Chinese been on a larger scale and better managed The same papers contain several proclamations, some of them immediately from the Emperor of China himself, commanding the Viceroy of Canton to put a stop to all foreign trade whatever, and to proceed to the utmost

BAST3X V3313W3283L 33523321103 AT23, extremities against the English ships. Every Englishman who shall be taken in the Chinese waters is forthwith to be given up to the authorities at Canton, and to be punishad as an outlaw trespassing on the domains of the Chinese empire. In another public Chinese paper, contained in the Canton Journal, the Viceroy solicits the Emperor of China to take into his imperial consideration, whether an immediate massacre of all Englishmen should not be ordered, þÿ or at least to such an extent as might strike terror into such as the imperial clemency might deem fit to spare. The concluding paragraph of this Chinese state paper is singular enough, and a good specimen of Chinese morals and policy. "Only let a plan be laid for a general massacre, and these said foreigners cannot but fear and tremble, and come to implore us. Afterwards, if we find that they can with a sinctre and contrite heart repent them of their crimes, then a memorial may be addressed to your sacred Majesty, praying that, out of the abundance of your heavenly goodness, you will again permit them to renew their commercial intercourse. But even then a limit must be put to the export of tea, rhubarb, and other commodities, and tlicy must on no account be permitted to exceed the prescribed bounds. This is what 1 call keeping a strong hold upon þÿthem literally the plan of the nippers. if, however, they dare afterwards clandestinely to convey opium into the inner land, then at one and the same time I would punish the offending parties with death, ac-
cording to the new statue, and again cut off" for ever their admission to our markets ; this then would most certainly cut otf their greedy views and cleanse the fountain."

þÿ þÿOOO From the St. James's Chronicle' JuneS. The Paris papers of Thursday, along with the letter of our private correspondent of tfiat date, have leaciied us. Marshal Val- Iee's dispatch to the Minister of War dated May 27, giving the details of his operations from the 23th of April, has at length made its appearance in the Moniteur, and occupies from nine to ten columns of that journal. It appears to us to confirm the imputations of want of decision and foresight, ignorance of the movements of his enemy, and indifference to the s.itoiv and comfort oi his troops, which have been cast upon Marshal Valine's conduct by the French journalists. Our correspondent affirms that the recal of the Marshal has been decided on, and that General Cubieres or General Trezel is to succeed him. A telegraphic dispatch reached Paris on Thursday morning announcing the fall of Morella and the castle. The last stronghold of Cabrera surrendered to the Queen's troops on the 31st ult. No mention is made of Cabrera. All the garrison became prisoners of war. The intelligence from Constantinople comes down to the 17th ult. It confirms the dismissal of liaiil Pacha The Eastern question appears to become daily more perple .ed. The British squadron, under Sir John Louis, was at Smyrna on the 19th. Admiral Lalan de was expected there, with his squadron, in order to assist in the celebration of her Majesty's birth-day.

We learn from the Paris papers that the proposed removal of the remains of the Emperor Napoleon from St. Helena to Paris, continued to occupy the press and the Chambers The Chamber of Peers voted on Saturday the bill for the transference of the Emperor's remains by a majority of 117 against 3. On Thursday Louis Philippe, surrounded by bis ministers and all the officers of his staff, received, in the hall of the throne, the former Grand Marshal of the Palace, General Count Bertrand, who delivered into his Majesty's hands the Arms of Napoleon. They consisted of the sword worn by the Emperor at the battle of Austerlitz and the only one he had used since ; two pairs of pistols, richly inlaid ; the Roman sword he wore at the Champs de Mai ; a sabre which belonged to John Sobieski ; and a poignard, given by the Pope to the Grand Master of the Knights of Malta. Lavalette. The King, on receiving the aims, said þÿ " I recei -e in the name of the country the arms of the Einperor Napoleon, whose last wishes confided to you this precious store ; they will be faithfully preserved until the moment when I shall be able to place them in the mausoleum which is being prepared for him by the national munificence of France. " I consider myself fortunate in having been reserved to restore to the land of France the mortal remains of him who added so much glory to our military exploits, and to acquit the debt of our country by encircling his coffin with all the honours that were due to him."

The right of General Bertrand to the eclat attendant on the presentation of these relics to the nation has been denied bv the family of Bonaparte, and some documents have been published in the Capitole, which certainly go far to impugn it.

Madrid journals and letters to t he 31st ult. have re ached us. The Gazette records a rencontre at La Cenia on the 20th inst., of Gen O'Donnell and the troops under his command, with eight battalions and 200 cavalrv commanded by Cabrera in person. The Carlists are said to have been driven from their position with considerable slaughter ; the Queen's troops having lost only 70 men, among whom was the brother of General O'Donnell. A large quantity of military stores, along with the carriages of Cabrera, are said to have fallen into the hands of the Christinos. The Fco de Arragon to the 30th inclusive has reached us. The journal of the day preceding furnishes details of the operations which led to the capture of San Pedro Martin on the 25th ult. Unable to resist the tremendous fire of the Christino artillery the garrison offered to surrendci on condition of their being allowed to retire into Moreila. þÿ This was refused Whilst the negociations were going on, however, the troops attempted to make a sortie, in which they were repulsed with considerable loss. The only foreign news of the week is the reported death of the King of Prussia, who is either in fact dead, or in such a state as to tender it no indelicacy to consider him as past all hopes of recovery. He was in every respect one of the most extraordinary princes of his age; a grave, soher, and wise reformer ; but taught by fatal experience to oppose himself, firmly and steadily, to all the pernicious fallacies of the age in which he lived ; a friend to liberty so far as it regarded private life, but most justly and wisely opposed to its pretensions where it sought to spread anarchy, turbulence, and impiety, and to weaken the authority of government. Like Metternich, his leading maxim appears to have been, " All for the people, but not through the people." No popular government in a country circumstanced as bis was, but a government exercised by the sovereign and the state, so as to promote the people's best interests, could expect his countenance. This maxim of the ureal German diplomatist is certainly more sjiecious than sound, as it assumes a wisdom and purity in kings and ministers, which, however personally perhaps belonging to two or three individuals of this age, and verv possibly to the Prussian minister of this day, is not, as a general principle, to be reasonably expected in a class of men necessarily exposed to the seductions of supreme power and ambitious pursuits Under this maxim, however, the King of Prussia steadily opposed himself to parliaments and

popular assemblies. To conciliate the people for refusing to accede to their wishes in this respect, he spared no eff >rt to bestow upon them eveiy other boon, and every public and private blessing. As regarded his officers, and almost his private soldiers, he laboriously inquired into every man's private circumstances and condition ; administered to their domestic comforts, and not unfrequently assisted them bv gifts and loans ol money He received everv petition from every person, and answered, as many as he could. He appeared in the streets with the dress and simplicity of a private gentleman ; defending himself onlv bv gravity and propriety of manners, and bv the Jove and esteem which this kind of conduct, added to his known kindness and reputed wisdom and virtue, universal) procured (or him He took also the right way to be faithfully served, and to be heartily beloved. bv his ministers, household, and numerous personal friends, amicus qreerens amando, seeking love by love; doubling liis benefits by the manner of bestowing them, and liberally and magnificently giving, not, as the French say, en maitre, as a master, but in all cases as a friend. In this way perhaps no sovereign of the day has left behind him a better name, or better realised the well-known line of the Roman pool, that þÿ ' nunquem libei las gratior extut , qumn sub rege pio."

ATTEMPT TO KOK VI V CHINESE NAVY. 'The Admiral Kwan's victory' at Chuenpee, on the 3d of November last, over her Majesty's ships Volage and Hyacinth, in which these came away without the slightest hurt, whilst a number of junks were blown up, sunk, and desiroyed, seems to have led the Imperial Commissioner to the conviction, that if lie should be obliged to report any . more such victories to his government, tie |

JTaM3irB33:R JR3p will be left without a naval force, and he has, therefore, it seems, determined on possessing himself of large foreign merchant ships, wherewith to oppose tlie English naval power. þÿ One ship, lately the Cambridge, now we believe the Chesapeake, under American colours, has already been purchased by the Chinese for 30,000 dollars, we hear ; in fact, her being allowed to enter the river at all, and dispose of her cargo, was, we are told, made conditional on her sale. The Chinese are treating for the purchase of otlier vessels likewise, and wished also to buy two Danish ships, the Danske Kotige and Norden (late j Vansittart and Mithras), but not being able j to arrange matters to their satisfaction with the owners, the imperial commissioner lias j hit upon an easier mode of possessing himself | of these vessels, as will be seen from the edict, in which he decrees the confiscation of the Danske Konge for no other reason but that she has come to Whampoa without erasing from her stern her former name, although lie confesses, in the same edict, that on application having been made lor that vessel proceeding to Whampoa, the circumstance of her change of ownership and flag had been stated The other vessel, the Norden, is confiscated, not because she luid a wrong name at her stern, but because she had none at all, and tins the Chinese discover now that tliey want the ship, though that same vessel, without a name on her stern, has often discharged and taken in cargo at Whainpoa. These

despotic and unprincipled acts of the Chinese, in making laws lor the occasion, proves to us daily more the necessity there was for the foreign merchants, after their imprisonment, leaving Canton until their safety shall be more guaranteed which it may not be in the power ot a Chinese Mandarin to break as caprice or avarice may prompt. Besides the three ships, the Cambridge, Danske Konge, and Norden, several other large country ships, now under the American flag, are spoken of as likely to be bought by the Chinese, who have also been desirous to contract for the building of a number of guri-boats after European models. We hope they may succeed to make a respectable show of fine vessels, and, should it come to open war between China and England, congratulate the naval officers of the latter upon the event.

Death or Paganini This celebrated vio- þÿ linist died at Nice on the 37th of May, after a lingering lilness. He has left one son, who inherits a large fortune. Paganini's remains were embalmed, to be removed to Genoa, his native town, for interment. The most wonderful performer on the violin has been taken from Hie musical world He had hosts of imitators, hut not one rival. He carried execution on the liddle beyond any former or subsequent (lerformer, and his almost demoniac feats of dexterity were only equalled by Ins touching lone, beautiful expression, impassioned feeling, and correct intonation. þÿ His compositions partook of his unearthly appearance ; his style was " sad by fits, by starts 'twas wild " His Witches' Danee was incomparably grotesque, eccentric, and true withal, and never did violin weep such strains as his " Nel cor piu" Paganini was avaricious, and little to be depended on in worldly affairs ; but some fits of generosity by which he was impelled have astonished even himself ile would never, it is said, forgive him-

He was engaged in the Casino speculation in Paris, but took fright and abandoned it, for which heavy damages were awarded against him, the payment of which he avoided bv his return to Italy, wfiere he died þÿ Morning Post.

Funeral op Sir Sydney Smith. þÿ The mortal remains of the gallant and illustrious admiral were interred in the Cemetery of Pere la Chaise on the 29th ult. The body was taken from his late residence in the Rue d'Aguisseau to the English Episcopal Church in the same street, followed by his relatives and many of the principal English residents in Paris, among whom we noticed several officers of high rank in the British navy. The introductory part of the service was performed in the church by the Right Rev. Bishop Luseonibe, and the body was (hen borne to the cemetery, attended by a long train of mourning and private carriages. Oa the pall was placed the hat and uniform of the deceased, and on a cushion his epaulettes and his several oiders. Over the foot of the coffin was spread the British union Jack. At the conclusion of the burial-service, which was most impressively read by Bishop Luscombe, three orations were delivered þÿ the first by M. Raoui. Avocat of the Court of Cessation, who, after pronouncing general a panegyric on the character of the deceased as a warrior, proceeded to eulogise hiin for his active and generous exertion in promoting the objects of several philanthropic societies of which he was a member, and to which his advice, his practical arid scientific acquirements, and his invention, were so invaluable. I he next speaker, M J ulien. gave a short but comprehensive recapitulation of the services of Sir Syndey, from liis'first entering the British navy at the age of 13, and also ex-

patiated largely on his amiable and philanthropic qualities. Both speakers were loud in their praise of Sir Sydney, for his having been almost the first to interfere for the suppression of European slavery in Africa, nud for his indefatigable and strenuous exertions in that humane cause The third gentleman, whose name we could not learn, spoke in a similar strain of eulogium of the character ol Sir Sydney as a citizen of the world ever ready to aid the cause of humanity. Some surprise was felt that, after these speeches had been delivered, none of his countrymen present should have come forward to pay a last tribute to his memory. No stronger testimony to his worth could, however, be shown than to hear his eulogiurn pronounced solely by members of a nation against w hich, in his career of arms he had so successfully and gloriously fought. No doubt this was owing to the absence of some previous arrangement, and to the want of any such custom in England. As Sir Sydney Smith was a member of the Legion of Honour, we expected to have seen a detachment of troop« escorting his body to the grave, and pei forming military honours over it, but this did not take place. þÿ Uulignam's Messenger.

V gentleman who left Yew Orleans May 1st, arid arrived at Cincinnati on the 11th, in the steam-boat Gen Brown, states that n ai' li/ the whole Jht country, from the mouth of the Ohio to New Orleans, is under water. Our advices from Yew Orleans to Mnv 9ih, represent the inundation in that vicinity to he already extensive, and the river still rising. The Picayune of that date contains the following ; By verbal accounts received vesterdav, we learn that the Ohio, Upper Mississippi, Missouri þÿ -in fact all the tributaries of the Mississippi are rapidly on the rise, and experienced man say that a general overflow is almost inevitable. At Lake Providence many of the plantations are now ov rflowed, and the rivetis breaking through at other places. Should our city overflow, and from the different statements and opinions of those acquainted, we think there certainly is great danger, it will be of incalculable injury. On falling.it leaves a thick sediment, which, independent of the injury merchandise would sustain, would be removed with difficulty and at an enormous expense. Let us river may stay where it is. Much as we j hope that the hate low water, we prefer it to an overflow. I | and Another New Orleans paper savs, þÿ - The authorities of the first have at length awakened to a sense of the < two of her children were killed in her arms danger to be apprehended from the encroachments of the river on the Levee, and have had an embankment constructed on that part

of the Levee nearly opposite the North American Hotel. It is however, but a feeble and inefficient barrier, and does not possess firmness ami solidity enough to resist a much further elevation of the Mississippi. THE TORNADO AT NATCHEZ. The New Orleans Picayune of the 10th inst. brings us some additional particulars in regard to this terrible þÿcalamity, as follows: Natchez, Thursday, 5 P. M. May 7. 7 o the Editors of the Daily Picayune By the steamboat Meteor 1 hasten to acquaint you with one of the most horrid and destructive hurricanes that ever happened in the United States. While nearly the whole of our city were engaged in dining at the hour of two this afternoon, vivid flashed the lightning, loud roared the thunder, and black grew the sky. In a few minutes the tempest came, and for about forty minutes we were in that perilous state which speaks only ofdestruction and death First toppled down the chiinriies, then went the roofs of houses, and a moment after house after house fell into ruins. In the hurry of this letter 1 cannot begin to particularize the death and damage around me. » Natchez under the bill" is entirely swept away, and the loveliest part of the South on the Bluff above, is wreck and ruin ; and those yet living will find difficulty upon difficuly in getting shelter to-night. heart sickens at the scenes before me. As My 1 walked to the boat irpm which I write, the

dead and wounded met me every twenty steps. Natchez, is ruined, ruined, ruined ! Yours, truly. In addition to the above we have gathered the following particulars. The steamboat St. Lawrence went down. It is said site was lifted many feet out of water and instantly dashed to the bottom of the river with every soul on board. The enormous bodv of water now rolling the Mississppi and swel- in ling to the very topmost limit of its banks, was lashed into foaming billows, and flatboats were torn to pieces ami their scattered planks flew about in the wind like feathers. The lady of Mr. Hallidav, one of the proprietors of the Free Trader, was saved by a miracle, with her young child in hei arms Every church and every public building shared in the ruin. Steeples were dashed to the earth, and houses all over the town were unroofed. The steamboat Prairie is now lying at our wharf torn to pieces þÿ " blown up" by the wind worse than ever boat was blow n up by steam. The hull and machinery is all that is left of her. Her cabin was carried away, floor and all. The wheel houses were unroofed, and what remains of the boat is rent and shattered in an awful manner. From the ruins of the steamboat Hotel, Mr. Alexander, the landlord, his lady and bar keeper, were dug out aiive, as adso Timothy Flint, the historian and geographer, his son from Natchitoches, La, besides ! Doctor Taliafero and many others Mrs municipality | Alexander is considered dangerously injured .

As many as nine dead bodies have been dug from the steamboat Hotel. The number of burials which took place on the Nth instant, was about fifty, and many are still in a dangerous and dying condition. From an estimate made by Mr. Raffner and S. J. Boyd, Esq , the total loss is supposed to be about $1,200, 000. The neighboring planters are generously sending in large gangs of slaves to assist in clearing the streets and digging the dead from the ruins. The greatest loss of life was among the flat boats, which were swamped and destroyed before the unfortunate men could escape to the shore. One paper states, upwards of 200 were lost A boy is said to have been taken up in the air and lodged in a tree halt a mile from his father's house. The citizens of Concordia and Madison have held a public meeting, and adopted measures for the relief of their friends in Natchez. This awful calamity has created a sensation here in New Orleans that will not soon be forgotten.

B.v the arrival of the Great Western, from Bristol, which place she left on the 4th, we have lull files of papers up to the day of her departure. We have only time to present our readers with those items of news which appear to be of the greatest interest and importance. The Great Western brings a large number of passengers, among whom are several Americans, with their families. The English news, so far as we have glanced at our files, is not very important. We learn from an authentic source that Mr. Hush, the Secretary of Legation at London, arrived in the Great Western, and that he departed immediately for Washington, being the bearer of important despatches from our Minister at London. Parliament had been doing nothing of great interest for several days. The Money Market, it will be seen by reference to the news uuder that head, continues easy and improving. The Bank of England has made its quarterly returns, which show a steady increase of specie in her vaults. We regret that the cotton market does not improve but has met with a further slight decline. The Epsom Races appear to engross the attention of all classes, as the Queen and Prince Albert attended them on the Derby Day. The most splendid preparations were made for their accommodation. A great meeting was held at Exeter Hall on the 1st inst , for theextinction of the foreign Slave Trade and the civilization of Africa. Prince Albert took the chair, and made a short and appropriate speech. Nearly 5000

men were present. The Queen's birth day was celebrated on the 25th ult. with great splendor. Her Majesty, through Lord Belhnvon, Chief Commissioner to the General Assembly of Scotland, has presented the munificent royal donation of £2000 for the propagation of the gospel in tire Highlands. There is an attempt to open the National Gallery and British Museum upon the Sabbath, for the accommodation of those persons who cannot visit these places during the week days. Courvoirier, the valet, and supposed murderer of Lord William Russell, has had his final examination, and is committed to Newgate to await his trial. The crops appear to he doing remarkably well throughout England, but trade is generally as bad as it can be. York Minister, a venerable and magnifi- , cent building at York, was destroyed by fire I

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, June 19, 1810. By the Great Western. Paris, June 1, 1840. The question of indigenous beet root sugar is at length put at rest by the imposition of such a protecting duty as will enable the colonist to come into the market without altogether ruining the home producer. The party of the late ministers have therefore been defeated in their attempt to suppress this important manufacture, for the silly purpose of assisting the colonists and of keeping those drowsy gentlemen in a state of indifference to the great improvements which have been ntade in the mother country. The last improvement consists in refining the beet root, and of course any other, sugar at the time of making it: by one continuous operation, without taking it from the mould until it is converted into the most beautiful lump. Such importance is attached to this discovery that it has obtained a prize of 20.000 francs. Your scientific readers may be pleased to know that by the use of alum in very small proportion, the principal part of the extraneous matters in the beet root juice are neutralized in a much more effectual manner than by the former process The beet root sugar, it may be well to note, is making rapid progress in Russia. If the United States would make of that manufacture a staple article, the slave trade would shortly die a natural death. The discussion of the sugar question naturally introduced a question as to the results of a maritime war in preventing supplies of colonial sugar to France. The president of

the Council and others gave a flattering picture of the present slate of the French navy, which tliev maintain to be superior to the English, The former superiority England ol is ascribed bv France to accidental circumstances which are not likely to recur The old revolution for instance was followed bv the disbanding of the naval officers, who at that time consisted of the old noblesse þÿ a new navy was consequently to be created. þÿ A French eighty gun ship of the present day is affirmed in pour a broadside of 3200 pounds weight, while the English ship discharges only 2800. The shipping of England in numerical force is not twice as great as that of France, while it has four times as many points to defend. The sulphur queslion is likely to take a turn far more unfavorable to Naples than his Neapolitan majesty had reason to expect. Hostilities have indeed been suspended on the part of Great Britain, the Sicilian ships captured have been restored, on the understanding that through the mediation of France matters are to be amicably settled, but it is quite understood that England would not put her interests into the hands of a mediator without having previously ascertained the certainty of a favorable result. The King will pay the cost of his folly by indemnifying the English merchants in Sicily who have been virtually robbed by him. IN PARLIAMENT. The proceedings of the week commencing on Monday, May 18th, may be briefly told. The first three nights in the House of Commons were occupied in the debate on Lord Stanley's Irish registration bill. In the Commons, among the petitions presented was one from the radical parish of Marylcbone, for the impeachment of Lord John Russell ; the crime charged upon him was the establishment of an unconstitutional gendarmerie, under the name of the police force. Amid much laughter the petition was ordered to lie on the table. The session was devoted to the adjourned debate on Lord Stanley's Irish registration bill, the motion being to go into committee on the bill. After long and able speeches from Mr. O'Connell, Sir Robert Peel, Lord Morpetli and others, the motion prevailed by a majority of 3 þÿ the vote being 301 to 298. Another ministerial defeat, but not so bad as the former on the same bill. We venture to say that the bill will be ultimately defeated In the lower house the 4th of June was fixed as the day for going into committee on Lord Stanley's Irish registiation bill, and the 12th for Lord John Russell's bills on the same subject. In the Commons Mr. Villiers again ofTered his motion for the repeal of the corn laws. þÿ The Spectator sa vs that " a mob of members met to raise a clamor against the motion, and succeeded in preventing discussion. Noise and tumult prevailed during part of the session, and several members rose, and resumed their seats, without being able to gain a hear-

ing. The landed gentlemen were strong in numbers as in lungs ; and a majority of 300 to 177 recorded their determination to maintain the grievance." Mr Hull moved for a committee to inquire into the expediency of permitting flour to be manufactured in bond, under what restriction this should be permitted. After a not very long debate the motion prevailed 126 to 54. þÿ

An extensive forgery has been discovered, by which two bankers of Lombard street are serious sufferers The delinquent, who has hitherto borne a first rate character as a man of business, has been largely engaged as a wholesale manufacturer in London, having three establishments in various parts of the metropolis, and two in large provincial towns.

British Steamers. The Britannia, one of Mr. Cunard's line, is advertised to depart from Liverpool for Halifax positively on the 1st of July. THE GREAT ARCTIC PROBLEM SOLVED. The long mooted geographical problem of a North Western Passage to the Pacific Ocean from the Atlantic, is at length solved, there is such a passage. The honor of this discovery belongs to Messrs. Dease & Simpson, ol the Hupson's Bay Company. In 1837, and again in 1838, they attempted to complete the exploration of the Northern shore of this Continent, by descending Coppermine River, which empties into the Arctic Ocean þÿ in longitude about 110 West, and from its mouth proceeding Eastward unti| they should arrive at the Westernmost point reached by explorers from the Atlantic. In both years they skirted along a great extent of coast, though much impeded by ice, but failed to accomplish the grand object of their pursuit. Now at length their perseverence has been rewarded. They have ascertained that Boothia is an Island, and that it is separated from the main-land by a strait from 3 to 10 miles wide, which connects the Gulf of Boothia, (partially explored by the Fury and llecla,) with the Arctic Ocean, in about lat, 68 33, and long. 98 10. The entire passage from the mouth of Coppermine River to the Atlantic, (extending near 50 degrees of longitude.) lies to the Southward of lat. 69. Leaving one ot our Ijiile craft, together with the remains ol the pemican (which through age and long exposi re was become quite mouldy,) and various other articles, as a prize to the first Esquimaux who mav visit the Bloody Fall, we ascended the river with our double crew in lour days, abandoned our tents, and every thing but absolute necessaries, crossed the barren grounds, up to the knees ity snow, having unluckily left our snow shoes on the coast, and saielv reached Fort Confidence at dusk on the 21lh. Our passage of Great Ccai Lake was most boisterous and inclement. In crossing the bodv of the Lake, and other considerable traverses, our boats, with every tiling in them, and even the very clothes on onr hacks became converted into shapeless masses and concretions of ice. It was L ig li time lor us to escape from Great Bear Lake, for the temperature, which was at 4 deg. below zero, when we landed at the head of the river, pi) the evening ol the 4th of October, fell 10 (leg. lower in the course of the night, and tiie neift day we descended the rapid stream in the very midst of the driving ice. On enteiing the Mackenzie, we experienced a temporary mitigation of this excessive cold ; but yvp should most assuredly have stuck fast above Fort Norman, had not the northern gains

again rose in their strength, and while they shattered and dispersed the rapidlv foimjng iee, enabled us to stand the current under close- reefed sails. By a very simple contrivance of stop cocks, &za., on the apparatus, the steamer can be turned on either course, retarded, stopjied, or have her motion reversed. This will be literally a revolution in the art of steam navigation.

HORRIULE MURDER OF LOUD WILLIAM RUSSELL. Yesterday morning, the west end of the town was startled by the discovery that Lord William Russell, brother to the late Duke of Bedford, and uncle to the noble Colonial Secretary, had been murdered in bed during the previous night, at his residence in Norfolkstreet, Parklane. The lamentable occurrence has created a most powerful sensation throughout the metropolis, and during the whole of yesterday Norfolk-street was crowded with persons of distinction anxious to gain accurate inlormation respecting the horrid affair. As is usual in cases of this character, a vast number of rumours were in circulation, but nothing, we believe, has hitherto been elicited beyond the facts sworn to at the inquest.
