OiN the occasion of their Royal Majesties, our most gracious Sovereign King CHRISTIAN the Eights, and our most gracious Queen CAROLINE AMALIA'S coronation, which solemnity will take place at the Koyal Palace of Fredericksborg on Sunday the 28th instant, the day is to be celebrated in all His þÿMajesty Westindia s Islands. During divine service, which, on this day, is to be publicly celebiated in all churches, it becomes the duty of all Ministers to direct the thought of their respective congrega. tions to the high importance of the day, and to beseech the Almighty to bestow þÿHeaven s choicest blessing on this our much beloved Koyal Pair. At sunrise the festival will be announced by the display of colours at all the Forts, on board the Vessels of War and the rest of the Shipping, also by firing from all Batteries salutes ot three times the number of Cannons mounted on them. The day happening to be Sunday no military parade will take place, to the end of not preventing the Inhabitants from attending divine service with their families.

With the exception of a Guard of //onour, to be stationed before Government house, during a Levee, to be held subsequently, the rest of the Garrison are to appear at Church, Divine service will commence at 11 þÿo clock | after which, at the Levee at 1 þÿo Clock,the Governors will receive the congratulations of all public officers and inhabitants, on the oc casion of their Koval Majesties' coronation. A salute from all the Forts like that of the morning, and a Koyal salute of 27 guns tron each of the Vessels of War will respond to the toast then festively given to their Majesties. At sunset a similar salute is to be repeated from the respective Forts. In the evening, at 8 þÿo Clock,Fireworks, procured by Vice Governor General, Chamberlain v. Sobotkbr and spared for this particular occasion, will be exhibited on the Quay. Music, perform ed on the wharf by the Military Band, will, on the part of the public, close the eelebration of the day. In consideration, that many members of the principal churches, most graciously tole rated in this Island, do not dance on Sunday, and for the purpose of preventing differences of creeds from being any impediment to lha participation of the general joy felt here on this festive occasion, as well as in the mother country, a ball will be given at Government house on the succeeding Monday, the 29Ul instant. It being the object, as much as possible to diffuse joy and hilarity over this festive day, and feeling myself called on to give the crew

of the vessel, on board of which I have accomplished so pleasant a passage from Europe, a token of my acknowledgement, a ball will be arranged on Tuesday, the 30th inst, iu the Barrack of this place. The Garrison as well as the Crew of both Vessels of War will there find opportunity of expressing their jov, and by the concord and good order, which will be observed, add to the exalted importance of the day. In the firm assurance that each and every one will know, in his circle, to celebrate this important day, we will unite with our brethren in the mother country, and, for the prosperity of Denmark and her Colonies, join in the wish :
Long life To their Majesties, the King and the Queen, and all the Royal Family. Goiyernment General of the Danish Westindia Islands, St. Croix the þÿ2 id of June 1 840.

Bearer of His Majestys most gracious answer to the congratulatory addresses, the Burgher Council and Planters of these Colonies have directed to His Majesty, on the occasion of His Majesty's accession to the throne, this commission becomes the dearer to me, as it, at tire same time, most graciously has pleased His Majesty personally to empower me, on my arrival here, to assure all His Majestys faithful and loyal subjects in these Colonies of His Majestys royal benevolence and grace. Each and every one will find in our new Sovereign an equally paternal and just monarch, as in our deceased King Frederik the Sixth of blessed memory. The public safety of these Colonies will find in His Majesty King Christian the Eight a protection equally firm, as His Majesty likewise, by every possible means, will seek to further the prosperity and happiness of these Islands. prosperous result of regulations, only ealeu' la led to the safety of these Islands aud to the welfare of the whole.

Thursday, July lti. þÿ The Lord Chancellor introduced the Regency bill After a preamble of some length his lordship said. Paris, July 22. The all absorbing topic of the day is the Syrian insurrection, and the waning power of Mehemet. Whatever be the immediate result of that event, whether it be suppressed or not by his preponderating force, it must have a material effect in acelerating the solution and education of India, for the wishes of the I of the Eastern question in favor of the Porte. good are with you ; go on in your great I During seven years that Mehemet has governed Syria, this is the third insurrection which has broken out in presence of considerable military force. Each time the revolt was quelled, partly, indeed, by force of arms, but chiefly by the magnificent promises ol Ibrahim to the mountain chiefs, bis most determined enemies. On the second revolt of the I) ruses the Egyptian troops were at first beaten, but Ibrahim, by a master stroke of policy, contrived to arm the Christians of the mountain against the infidels, and came off conqueror; his own weapons are, however, turned against him; the Christian population is in arms, and although not yet supported by the Druses who are bis ancient foes, they are said to have blockaded the Egyptian troops within their fortresses Nothing, in fact, seems necessary to their success but a union with the Druses.

A portion of the English fleet is sent to cruise þÿoff the Syrian coast, and the Porte is averred to be silently marching troops toward the scat of action from Gallipolis and Constantinople. The waning power of the Egyptian viceroy may 1 think be inferred in part from the abandonment of Arabia, which had cost him thirty years of combat and pecuniary sacrifice to conquer At retain, but which lias now virtually lallcn into the bauds ol Great Britain.

From the London Globe, July 24, evening. We learn with pleasure that the mischief apprehended from the stoppage of the Commercial Bank of England is now arrested ; as that Bank, in addition to redeeming her notes at sight, has actually taken up all over due bills bearing her signature as endorser or otherwise: thus relieving the holders from further trouble or anxiety about them. It now j only remains to satisfy her depositors, which we believe will not he very difficult, the liabilities under that head being moderate in amount. THE REVENUE.

On the year the deficiency in the Postoffice is £558,000 and there is a trifling deficit in the receipts from the Crown I .and Taxes and Miscellaneous luxes. llio penny postage of course, accounts for the deficit in the Postoffice, but that is nothing like so great as was prognosticated by the enemies of this great national boon. The number of letters continues steadily on the increase, and there can he no doubt that the revenue from this source will ultimately he as great as it ever was.

There is no subject of more momentous interest to every civilized nation, than an enquiry into the present position of England ; there is no topic of higher importance (socially speaking) to the whole family of man, than an endeavour to ascertain the future prospects of England. The first branch of enquiry would involve an investigation of proximate and remote causes of almost indefinite extent, and, on this occasion, an exposition of results is all that can be expected, reserving for a subsequent period, more minute, and, perhaps, more satisfactory details. One of the most prevalent existing opinions is, that England has witnessed the acme of her power, and, having passed the meridian, now hastens to decay. This inference is erroneously drawn, from observing, 1st, that individuals of the animal aud vegetable kingdoms have their periods of youth, age, and death ; and, 2d. that all the great nations of antiquity have perished, leaving scarcely a vestige of their name, the antiquary with difficulty tracing the spot on which the metropolitan cities of vast empires once stood. But the inference is unsubstantiated in its premises, and not fairly supported in its con. elusions. Examine one ot the primeval for. ests ot America þÿ it has existed there for ages ; its limits defined from the adjacent prairie by a broad and clear savanna, on which not a shrub is seen. True, the individual trees of of the forest perish, but their place is imme-

diately filled up ; ages roll on þÿ tree succeeds to tree þÿ the forest never becomes the prairie þÿ and at the end of centuries is found in all its beauty, denseness, and vigour. The same principle is applicable to herds of animals, and to congregrated masses of our fellow-creatures. Thus, also, is it with a nation : individuals die þÿ the nation lives, and will continue to flourish for ages, so long as gale j the elements of moral disease are subdued by virtue. The analogy, therefore, between the existence of an individual of a species, and the aggregate of a nation, is incorrect ; as also is the conclusion drawn from the supposed analogy. Empires, kingdoms and republics have risen from infancy to maturity, and then petished No form of government, whether that of absolutism, or democracy, has been found sufficient to save a nation from final extinction ; the seeds of dissolution were sown at birth, and were involved when the physical and intellectual structure began to wane. Babylon and Nineveh þÿ Egypt and Jerusalem þÿ Tyre and Carthage Athens and þÿ Borne þÿ have all in succession risen from insignificance into power, and then vanished like the þÿ baseless fabric of a vision," leaving scarcely a þÿ wreck þÿbehind. Let us n >w glance at the condition ol the transmarine provinces of the empire : where do we find peace and contentment ? it was the sarcastic remark o! a nohieinan who filled, within the Inst few years, the office of Secretary ol State for the Colonies that the " on lit Colony in tranquility was, Heligoland /" We pass without comment the questions of the stale of þÿCanada of the West Indies þÿ the East Indies, &c , they are well deserving of the most serious attention, and calculated to excite the most anxious solicitude; but we do not desire to make such topics mere parly questions, and our future numbers will contain ample discussions respecting their p ditical and social wants The condition of our Colonial possesions as well as that of our domestic state, is not the result merely of v 'sterday, but the sequence ol causes, some ol which are of lang standing, and the effects ot which though otien predicted, have always been neglected. J'he unfriendly bearing of our foreign relatious, is what may naturally be expected from rivals jealous o! our political power þÿ thirsting for our territorial wealth, and desirous of enriching themselves at our expense. There is not a kingdom in Europe, nor a republic in America, in actual friendly alliance with us ; and were a general war to occur, England would of possess an ally, unless self interest prompted a co operation. Many, indeed, of the continental nations would re-

joice in the destruction of the British Empire, as if they expected to rise on its ruins In the midst of these surrounding perils, we see no etlorts made by genious and wisdom, to avert impending evils ; temporary expedients are resorted to, and the energy and abilities of the country are wasted on acrimonious strife, and directed to no grand or definite principle for the preservation of the Social edifice, and the maintenance of integrity of the empire. Yet, however gloomy may be the present, there is 110 real cause of alarm for the future ; from the very nettle danger, we may pluck the fl >wer safety ; and out of the destructive elements around we may gather the means of advancing, securing, and establishing our power for ages Ii is true that we are en. deavouring to pay in gold, at £.'. 17s. 10 \d. an ounue. a debt of £800,000,000, contracted in a depreciated paper currency; and that £10,000,000, animal taxes are required to of pay simply the interest of that debt, without the accumulation of any sinking-fund towards its final liquidation But the property in the United Kingdom is almost incalculable. That of land alone is estimated at two thousand millions sterling ! England is not, therefore, insolvent; and whenever an able financier chooses to grapple with this vital subject, there are ample means for its adjustment. Of the 28,000.000 inhabitants in the United Kingdom, nearly 20 000,000 are unfortunateiv living from » hand to mouth," by precarious labour and scantily supplied with the
necessaries of life. Yet tins very abundance of labour may he rendered of the utmost value, was there perfect freedom of commerce, a tut no monopoly of the money which

legitimately represents trade; in other words, were there equal laws of freedom for the transfer ot commodities, and of there representative value. The great reform is now in process of accomplishment by the joint stock system of hanking, by means of which, if gradually and cautiously brought into operation, trade will be saved from future panics, and the country from ruinous vicissitudes in its monetary allairs Thus, steadiness of employment, and remunerative prices, will raise the value of property, and spread plenty throughout the land ; and when 20,000,000 of now half-fed, ill-clad, and imperfectly educated beings shall have been raised in the social scale, we shall daily find fresh sources of employment, and means will be multiplied for deriving the full benefits of the industry of intelligent, and morally disposed millions. But if we turn from the vast resources which England, Ireland, and Scotland possess in the fertility of the soil, and the highly civilized condition of the country; in the coai, iron, copper, lead, and tin, beneath its surface ; and in the productive fisheries around our shores ; if, while not overlooking these and many other elements of wealth and power, we view the transmarine possessions ol the empire, ' wide as ihe poles asunder ;" under nearly every parallel of latitude, and beneath almost every meridian of longitude, we behold myriads of human beings, of every creed, colour, and clime, and an incalculable immensity of every thing that can tend to

promote individual comfort and social pros perity. Do we require corn, whether wheat, barley, oats, maize, or rice; the vast plains of the Canadas, of Australia, and of India, offer an inexhaustible supply, independent of foreign countries, and of the casuality of adverse seasons. Every species of timber, may be obtained from our American and Asiatic possessions. The widely expanded downs of Austral- Asia, now covered with flocks of sheep, are becoming the wool country of the world. In the West and East Indies we have the means of supplying sugar, coffee, lea, cocoa, spices, &e. for all Europe. Cotton, flax, silk, indigo, and dye-stuff's are ready in limitless quantities, and at the cheapest rale. Tobacco, guns, hides, ivory furs, &c. are among the staples of our African possessions: wines, fruits, oil, and spirits, are obtainable in the colonies of Europe, as also in those of the southern hemisphere. India teems with gold, iron, copper, lead, and coal ; and in almost every settlement the grand adjuncts of commerce, coal, and iron, abound. We dwell not at this moment on the innumerable advantages which our colonies present ; we advert briefly to them, merely to indicate the riches that are at our doors, il we will hut wisely use them, and thus advance the happiness of mankind. With such unmined þÿwealth with such untasted abundance, it is folly þÿ nay, it is wickednes, to talk of England's decay ; she is but in the morning of her existence, bursting into light, and

betokening a golden harvest, not only for those of her own race and lineage, hut for all who desire the inappreciable blessings of a Christianized civilization. And this brings us to a consideration of the hostility of continental Europe. What has France, or Spain, or Portugal, to gain by the downfall of England? Do they think that constitutional freedom would be more secure

AVIS, against the encroachment of northern Europe, where the freest and most powerful kingdom on eaclt destroyed ? Were there even no Autocrat to threaten the people of the south and west with swarms of cossacks, Portugal would soon become an appanage of Spain, and Spain, in turn, would be added to the sovereignty of France, until the Gallic nation, incapable of maintaining so great a territorial dominion, would split into petty republics or oligarchies, and civilization would retrograde far more rapidly than it has advanced. On the other hand, would the despotic state of northern and eastern Europe long withstand the onward rush of a crusade for political liberty, if England were not a hand to check the misguided zeal of rash theorists for freedom. The determined enthusiasm of Germa. ny, and the reckless courage of Poland, would afford the means for kindling the flumes of foreign and civil war in Russia, Austria, and Prussia, I here is no longer a Holy Alliance in existence, to band nations together in self defence for some common purpose the balance of power among the different sovereignties <>f Europe is becoming daily less and less effective for the preservation of the rights of each: and if peace is to he preserved in Europe, and that war of opinion which Canning predicted is to be avoided, it must be by England preserving her puisance, and acting as the arbitress of the destinies of mankind.

In the confederacy of nations, as well as among the constituency of a kingdom, there must be some chief acknowledged, for the better upholding of the rights and privileges of each. I o which of the nations of Europe can that power be more safely entrusted than to England ' She belongs to Europe, although not on its continent ; she forms a part of the family compact of nations, yet has no personal interest in the connexion. Were the whole of Europe instantaneously engulphed by an earthquake. England would be no loser, territorially, commercially, or socially. But it is for the honour and advantage of England that Euiope should he in peace þÿ that its sovereigns and governments should by every possible means, extend freedom, knowleuge, and commerce. She lias a common interest in the welfare of Europe, as it contains the most civiliz< d portion of the human race ; but she can have no views adverse to the internal prosperity of France, Spain, Portugal, Austria, Russia, Prussia, «Vc, (To be concluded in our next.)
